segments.title: Atlantic trade shaped Canada's wartime navy
segments.body: The Royal Canadian Navy emerged from an interwar period in which near-disbandment and absorption into a single defence service had been serious possibilities. By 1945, it ranked third or fourth among the world's navies, depending on the measure used. Even the fourth-place estimate by ship numbers and tonnage describes a fleet without battleships or fleet carriers and with only a couple of light cruisers. Its strength lay in fighting the North Atlantic convoy and U-boat war. This was a navy organised to exercise sea control by protecting shipping while larger Allied forces secured command of the sea.

evidence.note: Interwar proposals to end naval independence, qualified third- or fourth-place ranking in 1945, and the distinction between gaining and exercising sea control.

segments.summary: Canada's wartime naval expansion produced a large convoy fleet whose strength lay in exercising sea control in the North Atlantic.

segments.title: Walter Hose preserved the naval service
segments.body: Walter Hose spent almost thirteen years fighting to preserve the navy as an independent service. His title changed from director to chief of naval staff after he won an initial round of that struggle. When the naval college and sailor-training establishment faced closure, he redirected some of their funding into the volunteer naval reserve. The reserve gave Canada an organisation around which its wartime navy could expand. Retaining that capacity required years of political resistance to dismantling the service.

evidence.note: Hose's nearly thirteen-year tenure, change of title, defence of service independence, and use of training funds for the volunteer reserve.

segments.summary: Walter Hose defended naval independence and redirected scarce training funds into a volunteer reserve capable of supporting wartime expansion.

segments.title: British sea power and Canada's trade-defence problem
segments.body: Reliance on the dominant maritime power reduced the apparent need for a separate Canadian defence effort. In this interpretation, the same habit had allowed the nineteenth-century United States to benefit from British naval strength. Dominion governments could point to Britain's battleships and question the cost of their own forces. Yet British command of the sea still had to be converted into the safe movement of goods during war. Canadian exports needed access to Britain, the United States, and other imperial markets, so escort provision served the Canadian economy as well as the Allied war effort.

evidence.note: Reliance on British maritime power, a nineteenth-century American comparison, and Canadian trade with Britain, America, and the wider empire.

segments.summary: British naval supremacy made local defence spending easier to postpone, but Canada's export trade still required escorts in wartime.

segments.title: Hose built a reserve culture for wartime adaptation
segments.body: Hose selected officers and NCOs to combine persistence with a willingness to improvise. The desired reserve culture paired holding the line with finding ways to accomplish an unfamiliar task. A colourful wartime anecdote attributes a submarine's capture to three Canadian sailors who boarded naked with pistols and reached its control positions. The imagined reaction of the German crew is part of the joke, rather than evidence about what they actually thought. Alex Clarke recognises the same combination of adaptability and stoicism in Canadian officers and reservists he has met.

evidence.note: Reserve leadership and institutional culture, the unnamed submarine-boarding anecdote, and Clarke's personal impression from meeting Canadian officers and reservists.

segments.summary: Hose's selection of reserve leaders encouraged improvisation under pressure, illustrated by a deliberately comic submarine-boarding anecdote.

segments.title: Type 26 and Canada's River naming tradition
segments.body: The Canadian Type 26 destroyer's River designation follows an older national naming tradition. Canadian wartime usage associated major rivers with destroyers and minor rivers with smaller vessels. Tribal and River were the prominent destroyer identities available for reuse. A recent Tribal class, the modern political weight of that word, and the Halifax class's city names made River the expected choice by elimination.

evidence.note: An explanation of the anticipated Type 26 class name through Canadian naming precedents and the political associations of Tribal.

segments.summary: Earlier River, Tribal, and city naming choices explain the expectation that Canada's Type 26 destroyers would use the River name.

segments.title: River covered several Canadian destroyer designs
segments.body: Canada's River designation grouped several destroyer designs under one national label. Saguenay and Skeena were A-class ships built for the Royal Canadian Navy. Transferred Royal Navy destroyers from several later prewar classes also received Canadian river names. River therefore identified a Canadian grouping without implying a single common design. These purpose-built and transferred ships provided the early basis for the navy's expansion.

evidence.note: Saguenay and Skeena and the mixed prewar destroyer designs called Rivers. Several subsequent transfer names are garbled or inconsistent, so individual renaming pairs are not asserted.

segments.summary: The Canadian River destroyers included purpose-built A-class vessels and transferred Royal Navy ships from several different designs.

segments.title: Victoria volunteers preceded the formal naval reserve
segments.body: Hose's effort to secure destroyers required lobbying in London and across Canada. His reserve-building work began on a smaller scale, with a company of Victoria businessmen and yachtsmen formed in 1913. The formal Royal Canadian Naval Volunteer Reserve followed in 1922 in this chronology. An informal local initiative thus preceded the reserve's establishment as part of the naval service. Hose's work on ships and personnel continued together before Nelles inherited the task.

evidence.note: Hose's lobbying, the 1913 Victoria volunteer company, and the formal reserve establishment dated to 1922 in the lecture.

segments.summary: Hose combined a campaign for destroyers with reserve organisation that grew from Victoria volunteers into a formal naval institution.

segments.title: Percy Nelles confronted industrial readiness
segments.body: Percy Walker Nelles took charge in January 1934 and spent the next decade pressing for expansion. His procurement plans met opposition from those resisting defence spending and those demanding Canadian construction instead of British purchases. He favoured domestic production but challenged its advocates to identify yards and turbine works capable of delivering destroyers in time. Skilled workers alone could not supply the large machinery needed to manufacture the equipment. Buying and installing that machinery required public investment, which the government was reluctant to provide. National procurement ambitions therefore ran ahead of the industrial facilities needed to fulfil them.

evidence.note: Nelles's 1934-1944 leadership and disputes over the skilled labour, heavy machinery, turbine production, and shipyards required for domestic destroyer construction.

segments.summary: Percy Nelles argued that Canadian shipbuilding ambition required investment in turbines, machinery, yards, and production capacity before a crisis.

segments.title: Roman army spending also supported public works
segments.body: Roman military spending also funded a large civil-engineering workforce. Troops spent much of their time on public works, including projects that supplied water and helped move food. Those activities supported the bread and circuses associated with imperial rule. Providing those public needs helped sustain political stability, while disruption of the system contributed to imperial difficulties.

evidence.note: The Roman army's civil-engineering role, its contribution to water and food supply, and the political consequences of that system breaking down.

segments.summary: The Roman army's civil-engineering role links military spending with water, transport, and food-distribution infrastructure.

segments.title: Shipyard investment offered Depression-era employment
segments.body: Nelles's case for shipyard investment included economic benefits beyond naval construction. Better-equipped yards would provide employment during the Depression and be ready to sell merchant ships when trade recovered. Governments favouring lower taxes and restrained spending resisted that argument. War eventually exposed the limits of relying on British resources. Treaty restrictions had constrained Royal Navy construction during the interwar years, leaving less capacity to satisfy every Canadian requirement.

evidence.note: Depression-era spending resistance, Nelles's employment and merchant-ship argument, and the limits of British naval resources under interwar treaty constraints.

segments.summary: Investment in Canadian yards promised employment and future merchant-ship business, while reliance on a treaty-limited Royal Navy carried wartime risks.

segments.title: Archive access shaped the Tribal destroyer book
segments.body: Alex Clarke limited his book's treatment of Canadian and Australian Tribal destroyers because COVID restrictions prevented visits to their primary archives. He chose a mainly British Royal Navy focus, including the other navies where their ships worked with British Tribals. His standard for the book required direct access to primary documents instead of constructing the account entirely from other historians' books. He distinguishes that research choice from his teaching videos, whose broad subjects often require secondary works. Subsequent archive visits made additions to a future edition possible, without a commitment that they would appear.

evidence.note: Clarke's personal account of COVID archive restrictions, his book's British emphasis, different source use in teaching, and possible future additions.

segments.summary: Primary-archive access determined the scope of the Tribal destroyer book, while the teaching videos draw more widely on secondary literature.

segments.title: Admiralty advice met Canadian political ambiguity
segments.body: British naval advice changed as strategic requirements changed. Canadian public promises and private intentions also gave Admiralty planners different signals about what the government would actually support. Advice framed around one could conflict with the other. One proposed explanation for the resulting friction is that Canada's Atlantic proximity encouraged British expectations of political similarity. In that interpretation, Australia's distance made different local requirements easier for British planners to accept.

evidence.note: The Sea Bound Coast as a reference for Canadian naval-policy debates, changing Admiralty advice, and a tentative Canada-Australia explanation based on distance and expectations.

segments.summary: Changing requirements and a gap between Canada's public promises and private intentions help explain apparently inconsistent Admiralty advice.

segments.title: Wartime expansion favored smaller escorts
segments.body: The wartime navy passed through roughly 1,150 ships and vessels while expanding from about 1,820 personnel to 96,000. The 1945 comparison counts vessels commissioned at any point during the year, so its totals are not a fleet snapshot for one date. Some destroyers had already decommissioned before others entered service. The figures include 24 destroyers, 68 frigates, 112 corvettes, 67 minesweepers, 75 motor launches, and 30 motor torpedo boats. Escorts and coastal craft supplied most of this expansion. Their task was to turn Allied sea control into the safe use of maritime routes.

evidence.note: Approximate wartime ship and personnel totals, escort and coastal-vessel counts, and the explicit warning that 1945 totals combine ships serving at different dates.
A fleet of smaller ships organised to exercise sea control.

segments.summary: The RCN expanded from about 1,820 personnel to 96,000 by concentrating on destroyers, frigates, corvettes, minesweepers, and coastal craft.

segments.title: Flower corvettes followed a mobilization timetable
segments.body: The planning rationale for Flower- and Hunt-class orders assumed war from 1942 onward. That date followed the 1932 end of the Ten-Year Rule in the interpretation offered here. Allowing roughly two years for construction and another year for work-up meant ordering light escorts about three years before the anticipated conflict. Apparently late prewar orders could therefore fit the navy's prescribed assumptions. The actual outbreak of war arrived ahead of that timetable, while further Flower orders followed in batches.

evidence.note: Prewar Flower and Hunt orders and the explanation connecting the Ten-Year Rule's 1932 end, an expected 1942 war, and construction plus work-up time.

segments.summary: An expected 1942 conflict, two years of construction, and a year of work-up explain the timetable behind prewar Flower and Hunt orders.

segments.title: Snowberry's construction, transfer, and forecastle refit
segments.body: Snowberry was ordered in January 1940, laid down in February, launched in August, and commissioned into the Royal Navy in November. Initial British service included convoy trips before her transfer to the Royal Canadian Navy in May 1941. She remained in Canadian service until June 1945. Her forecastle was extended in May 1943 as part of a wider set of modifications. The photograph discussed shows the ship after that alteration, so it depicts a later configuration than the one in which she entered service.

evidence.note: Snowberry's construction and service dates, May 1943 forecastle extension, and the stated post-refit date of the photograph. The yard location in the captions is unclear.

segments.summary: Snowberry moved from rapid construction and British service to Canadian convoy work, with a 1943 refit changing her visible configuration.

segments.title: Snowberry moved where escort pressure was greatest
segments.body: After work-up at Greenock and Tobermory and duty with Western Approaches Command, Snowberry moved to Newfoundland. She escorted convoys between St. John's and Iceland, where North Atlantic wear led to a refit in February 1942. Subsequent assignments took her through the Oceanic Escort Force and Western Local Escort Force. Tanker protection then became a priority, and she served under American control on the Guantanamo-New York route. Britain and Canada supplied escorts because American convoy arrangements lacked enough vessels. Snowberry's movements followed changing demands across Allied commands.

evidence.note: British work-up, Newfoundland Command, the St. John's-Iceland route, February 1942 refit, and changes of escort force.
Tanker priority and Canadian and British escorts under American control between Guantanamo and New York.

segments.summary: Snowberry's assignments trace the changing Atlantic escort problem from Newfoundland convoys to local defence, tanker protection, and service under American control.

segments.title: Western support forces reinforced threatened convoys
segments.body: The Western Local Escort Force answered the increased patrol and convoy demands of the Second Happy Time. Flowers, Bangors, and some upgraded Town-class destroyers supplied its ships. Destroyers later moved into the Western Support Force to reinforce the regular escort groups. The local organisation comprised roughly eight escort groups and three or four support groups. A convoy retained its own escort, while intelligence about approaching submarines could bring additional support. For a merchant crew, the arrival of larger destroyers was reassuring firepower and a warning that a wolf pack might lie ahead.

evidence.note: The Second Happy Time response, participating ship types, approximate local group numbers, and intelligence-directed reinforcement of convoys.

segments.summary: Regular escorts stayed with convoys while support groups could reinforce routes threatened by submarine concentrations.

segments.title: Flower corvettes became a multinational escort type
segments.body: Britain supplied Flower-class corvettes to the United States within the wider Lend-Lease relationship. American aid overwhelmingly dominated that exchange, but vessels also travelled in the other direction. Wartime Flower operators included the British, Canadian, American, Free French, Free Belgian, Greek, Indian, Dutch, New Zealand, Norwegian, South African, and Yugoslav navies. Postwar use extended to further fleets, including Argentina, Chile, Denmark, Egypt, Israel, Ireland, and Thailand. The class's career therefore continued across many national services after its original wartime escort role.

evidence.note: British Flower transfers to America within a predominantly American aid flow, plus named wartime and postwar operators. The apparent Bolivian reference is not resolved.

segments.summary: Flower-class service crossed Allied national boundaries and continued in many postwar navies, with transfers to the United States illustrating reciprocal wartime aid.

segments.title: Snowberry and guided-weapon target priorities
segments.body: Snowberry joined Escort Group 5 in August 1943 after her major refit. The group encountered aircraft carrying the Henschel Hs 293 guided anti-ship weapon. Her small size probably made her a low-priority target compared with larger escorts, especially when the launch aircraft could remain beyond her effective anti-aircraft range. The comparison with using a modern hypersonic weapon against an offshore patrol vessel concerns target value and the availability of more worthwhile targets. Egret was sunk during these attacks, while several other ship and aircraft names in this account remain unclear.

evidence.note: Escort Group 5, Hs 293 attacks, the tentative small-target explanation, and stand-off launch range. The Asphodel/Athabaskan identification and aircraft wording require audiovisual clarification.

segments.summary: Snowberry's survival prompts an explanation based on target value, limited anti-aircraft reach, and German preference for larger escorts.

segments.title: Snowberry and experienced escorts sank U-536
segments.body: In November 1943, Snowberry helped sink U-536 with depth charges off the Azores. A frigate and two Flower-class corvettes brought experienced crews to the attack, leaving the submarine under sustained pressure. Calgary is named alongside Snowberry, while the frigate's name is unclear in the captions. Snowberry continued escort work before joining Portsmouth Command in September 1944 for Channel operations. After Canadian decommissioning, she was used as a target ship off Portsmouth in 1946 before scrapping.

evidence.note: The November 1943 U-536 attack by a frigate and two corvettes, followed by Portsmouth Command service and postwar disposal. The frigate is transcribed as Nepean and is left unidentified.

segments.summary: Experienced Canadian escorts overwhelmed U-536, and Snowberry later supported Channel operations before becoming a target ship.

segments.title: River frigates arrived for the late-war fight
segments.body: River-class frigates reached service late enough to help establish frigate as a common postwar escort designation. Prewar sloops and wartime corvettes preceded them, with American destroyer escorts serving a comparable role to frigates. Canada ordered thirty-odd Rivers in 1942, including Springhill in June. She was laid down in May 1943, launched that September, and commissioned in March 1944. The interval illustrates the two to three years needed to make a new escort operational. Typical outfits included two 4-inch guns, sometimes four, with 12-pounders and 40-mm or 20-mm weapons among the varying lighter armament. Crews adapted their equipment, and individual ships differed from the theoretical standard. Springhill's anti-submarine outfit included Hedgehog and 150 depth charges. These frigates represented the escorts that mass deployment of Type XXI U-boats would have faced if the war had continued.

evidence.note: Escort terminology, the 1942 River orders, and Springhill's June 1942 order to March 1944 commissioning.
The hypothetical Type XXI campaign, variable River gun fittings, Hedgehog, and 150 depth charges.

segments.summary: HMCS Springhill shows why the frigate became the enduring escort type and how long construction times pushed advanced escorts into the war's final phase.

segments.title: Escort, support, and hunter groups formed a ladder
segments.body: Springhill worked up in Bermuda before joining Escort Group 16, where convoy duty allowed further training. Ships with successful crews could progress to support or hunter groups. Escort groups stayed with shipping, support groups reinforced threatened convoys, and hunter groups were directed towards submarine concentrations using information such as radio emissions. Some hunter groups carried support-group labels to obscure their role. Approximate ratios were one support group for three or four escort groups and one hunter group for two support groups, with regional variation. Flowers could move between escort and support duties, while larger sloops, Black Swans, and some destroyers more often served in hunter groups. These preparations anticipated the possible mass arrival of Type XXI U-boats. Since that deployment never happened, their adequacy against it remained untested.

evidence.note: Springhill's Bermuda work-up and EG 16 assignment, crew progression, radio information, and hunter groups concealed under support labels.
Approximate and regionally variable group ratios, different ship types, crew proficiency, and the untested preparations for mass Type XXI deployment.

segments.summary: Crews and ships could progress from convoy escort groups into support or hunter groups as their anti-submarine proficiency increased.

segments.title: The Battle of the St. Lawrence forged ASW skill
segments.body: Cold fresh water meeting seawater made submarine detection in the St. Lawrence unusually difficult. Merchant ships still had to pass through the area, giving U-boats opportunities to exploit those conditions. Escorts gained demanding anti-submarine experience there or risked being sunk. Springhill's service in the area made her a strong candidate for Far Eastern duties in this assessment. In March 1945 she was ordered to Derry for conversion, with protection of assault convoys against submarines and possible suicide craft in view. Those duties anticipated an invasion of Japan.

evidence.note: St. Lawrence detection difficulties, Springhill's experience, and the rationale for a Derry refit for anticipated Far Eastern assault-convoy duty.

segments.summary: Springhill's experience in difficult St. Lawrence conditions helps explain her selection to protect assault convoys in the planned invasion of Japan.

segments.title: Springhill's Pacific refit ended in disposal
segments.body: Springhill was still undergoing her Far Eastern refit when the war ended. Work finished in October 1945, followed by payoff in December and disposal for breaking up in Nova Scotia in 1947. The navy abandoned the intended Pacific employment after investing in the conversion. Her disposal draws criticism because an escort of this kind would have been useful in the Korean War. That judgment links the later cost of lost capability with the rapid contraction after both world wars.

evidence.note: October 1945 refit completion, December payoff, 1947 breakup, and the opinion that retaining Springhill would have helped in Korea.

segments.summary: Springhill completed her Pacific conversion after the war ended, and her early disposal sacrificed a potentially useful Korean War escort.

segments.title: Tribal destroyers exposed the meaning of off the shelf
segments.body: Haida was ordered in 1940, laid down in 1941, launched in 1942, and commissioned in 1943. Her roughly three-year path to service depended on manufacturing turbines, guns, steel plate, and other long-lead items. An off-the-shelf design still requires that equipment to be ordered from factories. In this usage, the phrase describes a design whose components have active production lines that a buyer can join. Design availability therefore gives access to an industrial queue, with delivery dependent on its capacity.

evidence.note: Haida's construction sequence and the meaning of an available design whose long-lead equipment must still be manufactured.

segments.summary: Haida's three-year path to service shows that an existing design still depends on scarce production slots, turbines, guns, steel, and other long-lead components.

segments.title: Emergency orders hedged against two wars
segments.body: Nelles wanted Canadian destroyers ordered in 1938, but political delay held authorisation until 1940. Canadian orders consequently followed British prewar emergency orders and the further orders placed once war began. Haida was ordered in April 1940 and laid down in September 1941 despite using the established Tribal design. The British ordering rationale allowed for roughly three years before a ship entered service. If the European war continued, the ships would reinforce it; if it ended sooner, they would restore numbers for a possible war with Japan. Canada chose Tribals because they offered cruiser-like presence without the cost of cruisers. Delayed approval therefore affected when a familiar design could reach the fleet.

evidence.note: The delayed Canadian decision and its position behind British prewar and wartime emergency orders.
British orders as long-war reinforcement or postwar reconstruction before a possible Far Eastern conflict.
Haida's April 1940 order and September 1941 laying down, and the attraction of cruiser-like Tribal destroyers.

segments.summary: Late Canadian authorization placed its Tribals behind British emergency orders, while three-year build times made new ships insurance against both a long European war and a later Pacific conflict.

segments.title: Haida screened Arctic convoys at North Cape
segments.body: Early in her career, Haida joined the Home Fleet's Arctic convoy cycle. During the Battle of North Cape, she screened one of the convoys bound for Russia while other forces engaged Scharnhorst. Her destroyer group stayed between the merchant ships and the battleship's expected approach, ready to attack if it broke through. Some destroyer commanders regretted missing the surface action and appear to have thought their participation would have shortened it. The ensuing portrait of British, Canadian, Australian, and American destroyer officers deliberately exaggerates their confidence in tackling much larger opponents. Their aggression coexisted with the professional duty to remain on the convoy screen.

evidence.note: Haida's early Arctic convoy work and the destroyer screen's duty during North Cape. The precise number of her convoy trips is explicitly uncertain.
Reported frustration at missing the action and a humorous, exaggerated characterisation of Allied destroyer commanders' confidence.

segments.summary: Early in her career, Haida protected an Arctic convoy during the Battle of North Cape while heavier forces intercepted Scharnhorst.

segments.title: Haida's Channel sweeps and disputed T27 credit
segments.body: The 10th Destroyer Flotilla carried out Channel and Bay of Biscay sweeps connected with Operation Tunnel, Operation Hostile, and protection of the D-Day landings. Haida and Huron regularly outran the supporting cruisers Black Prince and Bellona to close German forces. Haida helped sink the Elbing-class torpedo boat T29 on the night of 25-26 April. On the night of 28-29 April she drove T27 aground and set it on fire with shelling intended to prevent recovery. MTB 673 also claimed credit, although the preference expressed here is to award the victory to Haida. These operations also included Haida's rescue of sailors from a ship damaged by a torpedo boat.

evidence.note: The 10th Destroyer Flotilla's sweeps, supporting cruisers, T29 and T27 actions, and the competing MTB 673 claim with an explicit preference for Haida.
Haida's rescue of sailors after a torpedo-boat attack. The rescued ship's name is garbled as Asdic and remains unidentified.

segments.summary: Channel sweeps brought Haida into repeated close actions against German torpedo boats, including the disputed credit for destroying T27.

segments.title: Haida and Huron pursued Z32 at Ushant
segments.body: At the Battle of Ushant, also called the Battle of Ile de Batz here, Haida and Huron pursued the German destroyer Z32. Z32 ran through a minefield and grounded while trying to escape. Sustained pursuit by the Canadian ships drove the German destroyer ashore. A deliberately comic interpretation treats that pressure as psychological intimidation of the opponent.

evidence.note: Z32's pursuit and grounding at Ushant or Ile de Batz, with humorous speculation about the psychological effect of Haida and Huron.

segments.summary: Haida and Huron's pursuit ended with Z32 passing through a minefield and grounding on the coast.

segments.title: Haida stayed in action after a gun-mount explosion
segments.body: During an August action, a shell exploded in one of Haida's gun mounts. It killed two sailors, injured eight, started a fire, and disabled the mount. Haida remained in the line of battle and continued engaging enemy vessels and shore batteries. A major refit followed from September 1944 into January 1945. New radar and other systems prepared her for further operations.

evidence.note: Haida's August gun-mount explosion, two killed and eight injured, continued combat, and September 1944-January 1945 refit.

segments.summary: A gun-mount explosion caused fatal casualties and a fire, but Haida continued fighting before a later refit upgraded her systems.

segments.title: Convoy RA66 survived a late U-boat attack
segments.body: Convoy RA66 faced a U-boat attack during one of the RCN's last major wartime engagements. The convoy's practised zigzagging caused the incoming torpedoes to miss. The escorts counterattacked, with HMS Goodall among the ships engaging the submarines. Two U-boats were sunk, but Goodall was also lost. The convoy otherwise passed through without losses, demonstrating the combination of merchant-ship manoeuvre and escort counterattack.

evidence.note: The late-war RA66 action, torpedoes missing a zigzagging convoy, two submarines sunk, and the loss of Goodall.

segments.summary: Trained zigzagging helped RA66 avoid torpedoes before its escorts counterattacked, losing Goodall while sinking two U-boats.

segments.title: Haida and Huron: Trondheim surrender duty and Pacific refit
segments.body: Haida and Huron frequently operated together, a partnership that prompts regret that both were not preserved side by side. Their final European duties included entering Trondheim with the Fifth Escort Group and a British ship to receive surrendering U-boats. In June 1945 they returned to Halifax for refits intended to prepare them for the invasion of Japan. Japan surrendered while that work was under way. The same ships therefore moved from European surrender duties into preparations for a campaign that never took place.

evidence.note: The wish to preserve both ships together, Trondheim with the Fifth Escort Group, and the unfinished Pacific refits. The accompanying British ship's name is garbled as Barric.

segments.summary: Haida and Huron's wartime partnership continued through Trondheim surrender duties and preparations for the invasion of Japan.

segments.title: Canada retained destroyers in postwar reserve
segments.body: Canada retained a number of its large destroyers, especially Tribals, after the wartime fleet contracted. Haida was paid off in March 1946 and placed in reserve. Decommissioning and storage kept such ships available for later recommissioning as requirements changed. The policy preserved selected fleet capacity through periods when the ships were not in active use.

evidence.note: Haida's March 1946 payoff and the broader practice of decommissioning, storing, and recommissioning Canadian Tribal destroyers.

segments.summary: Storing large destroyers allowed Canada to recommission selected ships when postwar requirements increased.

segments.title: Wartime readiness served a lasting trade need
segments.body: Hose and Nelles prepared the navy for expansion, particularly through the reserve, despite government reluctance to support their plans. Wartime growth then met Canada's need to move goods by sea. A recurring criticism is that successive governments lost sight of that requirement when trade flowed freely under a friendly maritime guarantor. Canada's imports and exports still depended heavily on shipping. The navy's convoy role gave practical effect to that economic need during war.

evidence.note: The roles of Hose and Nelles, criticism of peacetime government complacency, and the navy's purpose in supporting Canada's trade-dependent economy.

segments.summary: Reserve preparation supported wartime expansion, while Canada's dependence on seaborne imports and exports supplied the continuing reason for an escort fleet.
